mathematics.reason: Maths interpreter: FAIL. The Stability metric is defined as an average of terms of the form ‖g(xᵢ) − g(xᵢ′)‖² / ‖g(xᵢ)‖², where both numerator and denominator are squared norms. Squared norms are strictly non-negative for any real-valued vectors, so every term in the sum is ≥ 0, and the average is therefore ≥ 0. A lower bound of −1 is mathematically impossible under this definition: no assignment of real vectors can make the metric negative. The paper's stated range of [−1, 1] is thus inconsistent with its own formula. Wolfram could not evaluate the symbolic expression directly, but the conclusion follows immediately from the definition of a norm and requires no further computation.

judge_panel.reason: The abstract and Section IV mention 'various data types like tabular and image data,' but the actual experiments use only three tabular datasets (Iris, Wine, Breast Cancer Wisconsin). No image dataset experiments are reported anywhere in the paper, making the claim about breadth an overstatement.

The paper claims broader experimentation than it reports: the abstract says it assesses XAI methods "across multiple datasets and machine learning models," and Section IV says experiments encompassed "various data types like tabular and image data," but the listed datasets are only "Iris," "Wine," and "Breast Cancer Wisconsin," with no image-dataset experiment reported.

The paper claims to perform experiments "encompassing various data types like tabular and image data" (Section IV), but lists only three tabular datasets (Iris, Wine, Breast Cancer Wisconsin) and no image datasets, confirming the reviewer's concern.

judge_panel.reason: The paper explicitly states 'At the beginning of the benchmarking process, no specific domain is considered, so the weights will not be defined. These weights will be defined via surveys and questionnaires and will be applied in future work.' Coverage is defined in Eq. 4 but never reported in Tables I or II, and no scalar unified score is computed or demonstrated.

The paper does not actually compute a unified scalar score: it states, "the weights will not be defined. These weights will be defined via surveys and questionnaires and will be applied in future work," and the results say the scores were "computed based on fidelity, simplicity, and stability" only. Although "Coverage" is defined and a knowledge base is proposed, no experimental results for coverage, a weighted unified score, or a validated knowledge base are shown.

The paper acknowledges that the weights for the unified score "will be defined via surveys and questionnaires and will be applied in future work," and Tables I and II report only individual metrics (fidelity, simplicity, stability), confirming the score is not actually computed.
